# diesel_migrations 2.3.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/diesel_migrations/

Provides functions for maintaining database schema.

A database migration always provides procedures to update the schema, as well as to revert itself. Diesel's migrations are versioned, and run in order. Diesel also takes care of tracking which migrations have already been run automatically. Your migrations don't need to be idempotent, as Diesel will ensure no migration is run twice unless it has been reverted.

Migrations should be placed in a `/migrations` directory at the root of your project (the same
directory as `Cargo.toml`). When any of these functions are run, Diesel will search for the
migrations directory in the current directory and its parents, stopping when it finds the
directory containing `Cargo.toml`.

Individual migrations should be a folder containing two files, `up.sql` and `down.sql`.
`up.sql` will be used to run the migration, while `down.sql` will be used for reverting it. The
folder itself should have the structure `{version}_{migration_name}`. It is recommended that
you use the timestamp of creation for the version.

Migrations can either be run with the CLI or embedded into the compiled application
and executed with code, for example right after establishing a database connection.
For more information, consult the [`embed_migrations!`] macro.

## Transactions

By default, each migration runs inside its own transaction. This means a failing migration is automatically rolled back, leaving the database in the state it was in before the migration started.

You can disable this behaviour on a per-migration basis. For file-based migrations,
add a `metadata.toml` file to the migration folder with `run_in_transaction = false`.
See [`FileBasedMigrations`] for a full example and an explanation of the
"cannot run inside a transaction block" error that certain database operations produce.

---

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/diesel_migrations/latest

A database migration always provides procedures to update the schema, as well as to revert itself. Diesel's migrations are versioned, and run in order. # diesel_migrations - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/diesel_migrations/latest/aarch64-apple-darwin/diesel_migrations/

## Expand description

Provides functions for maintaining database schema.

A database migration always provides procedures to update the schema, as well as to revert itself. Diesel’s migrations are versioned, and run in order. Diesel also takes care of tracking which migrations have already been run automatically. Your migrations don’t need to be idempotent, as Diesel will ensure no migration is run twice unless it has been reverted.

Migrations should be placed in a `/migrations` directory at the root of your project (the same
directory as `Cargo.toml`). When any of these functions are run, Diesel will search for the
migrations directory in the current directory and its parents, stopping when it finds the
directory containing `Cargo.toml`.

Individual migrations should be a folder containing two files, `up.sql` and `down.sql`.
`up.sql` will be used to run the migration, while `down.sql` will be used for reverting it. The
folder itself should have the structure `{version}_{migration_name}`. It is recommended that
you use the timestamp of creation for the version.

Migrations can either be run with the CLI or embedded into the compiled application
and executed with code, for example right after establishing a database connection.
For more information, consult the [ embed_migrations!](https://docs.rs/macro.embed_migrations.html) macro.

[§](https://docs.rs#transactions)Transactions

By default, each migration runs inside its own transaction. This means a failing migration is automatically rolled back, leaving the database in the state it was in before the migration started.

You can disable this behaviour on a per-migration basis. For file-based migrations,
add a `metadata.toml` file to the migration folder with `run_in_transaction = false`.
See [ FileBasedMigrations](https://docs.rs/struct.FileBasedMigrations.html) for a full example and an explanation of the
“cannot run inside a transaction block” error that certain database operations produce.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [embed_](https://docs.rs/macro.embed_migrations.html)- migrations
- This macro will read your migrations at compile time, and create a constant value containing an embedded list of all your migrations as available at compile time. This is useful if you would like to use Diesel’s migration infrastructure, but want to ship a single executable file (such as for embedded applications). It can also be used to apply migrations to an in memory database (Diesel does this for its own test suite).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Embedded](https://docs.rs/struct.EmbeddedMigrations.html)- Migrations
- A migration source that embeds migrations into the final binary
- [File](https://docs.rs/struct.FileBasedMigrations.html)- Based - Migrations
- A migration source based on a migration directory in the file system
- [Harness](https://docs.rs/struct.HarnessWithOutput.html)- With - Output
- A migration harness that writes messages into some output for each applied/reverted migration

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Migration](https://docs.rs/trait.MigrationHarness.html)- Harness
- A migration harness is an entity which applies migration to an existing database

---

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

---

# Badges

Source: https://docs.rs/about/badges

Docs.rs no longer has its own badges. Consider using [shields.io](https://shields.io) instead.

---

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (4c9d2bfe4 2026-07-01)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

---

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

---

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

---

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# diesel_migrations 2.3.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/diesel_migrations/latest/builds

All the builds on docs.rs are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The limits for this crate are the following:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                    If a build fails because it hit one of those limits please
                    [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                    to get them increased.

# diesel 2.3.10 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/diesel/~2.3.0

# A safe, extensible ORM and Query Builder for Rust

API Documentation: [latest release](https://docs.rs/diesel) – [main branch](https://docs.diesel.rs/main/diesel/index.html)

Diesel gets rid of the boilerplate for database interaction and eliminates runtime errors without sacrificing performance. It takes full advantage of Rust's type system to create a low overhead query builder that "feels like Rust."

Supported databases:

You can configure the database backend in `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = {  = "<version>",  = ["<postgres|mysql|sqlite>"] }
```
## Getting Started

Find our extensive Getting Started tutorial at
[https://diesel.rs/guides/getting-started](https://diesel.rs/guides/getting-started).
Guides on more specific features are coming soon.

## Getting help

If you run into problems, you can come ask for help at in our [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/diesel-rs/diesel/discussions) forum.
This is also the right place to propose new features or show your applications.

## Usage

### Simple queries

Simple queries are a complete breeze. Loading all users from a database:

```
table.load
```
Executed SQL:

```
SELECT * FROM users;
```
Loading all the posts for a user:

```
belonging_to.load
```
Executed SQL:

```
SELECT * FROM posts WHERE user_id = 1;
```
### Complex queries

Diesel's powerful query builder helps you construct queries as simple or complex as you need, at zero cost.

```
let versions = belonging_to
  .select
  .order
  .limit;
let downloads = version_downloads
  .filter
  .filter
  .order
  .?;
```
Executed SQL:

```
SELECT version_downloads.* FROM version_downloads
  WHERE date > (NOW - '90 days')
    AND version_id = ANY(
      SELECT id FROM versions
        WHERE crate_id = 1
        ORDER BY num DESC
        LIMIT 5
    )
  ORDER BY date
```
### Less boilerplate

Diesel codegen generates boilerplate for you. It lets you focus on your business logic, not mapping to and from SQL rows.

That means you can write this:

```
```
Instead of this without Diesel:

```
```
### Inserting data

It's not just about reading data. Diesel makes it easy to use structs for new records.

```
let new_users = vec!;
insert_into
    .values
    .execute;
```
Executed SQL:

```
INSERT INTO users (name, hair_color) VALUES
  ('Sean', 'Black'),
  ('Gordon', DEFAULT)
```
If you need data from the rows you inserted, just change `execute` to `get_result` or `get_results`. Diesel will take care of the rest.

```
let new_users = vec!;
let inserted_users = insert_into
    .values
    .;
```
Executed SQL:

```
INSERT INTO users (name, hair_color) VALUES
  ('Sean', 'Black'),
  ('Gordon', DEFAULT)
  RETURNING *
```
### Updating data

Diesel's codegen can generate several ways to update a row, letting you encapsulate your logic in the way that makes sense for your app.

Modifying a struct:

```
post.published = true;
post.save_changes;
```
One-off batch changes:

```
update
    .set
    .execute
```
Using a struct for encapsulation:

```
update
    .set
    .execute
```
### Raw SQL

There will always be certain queries that are just easier to write as raw SQL, or can't be expressed with the query builder. Even in these cases, Diesel provides an easy to use API for writing raw SQL.

```
// Using `include_str!` allows us to keep the SQL in a
// separate file, where our editor can give us SQL specific
// syntax highlighting.
sql_query
    .
    .
    .
    .?;
```

# cfg-if

A macro to ergonomically define an item depending on a large number of #[cfg] parameters. Structured like an if-else chain, the first matching branch is the item that gets emitted.

 = "1.0"
```

cfg_if!
```

```
```

# dotenvy 0.15.7 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/dotenvy/^0.15

# dotenvy

A well-maintained fork of the [dotenv](https://github.com/dotenv-rs/dotenv) crate.

This crate is the suggested alternative for `dotenv` in security advisory [RUSTSEC-2021-0141](https://rustsec.org/advisories/RUSTSEC-2021-0141.html).

This library loads environment variables from a *.env* file. This is convenient for dev environments.

## Components

- `dotenvy`- `dotenv`crate.
- `dotenvy_macro`- `dotenv_codegen`.
- `dotenvy`CLI tool for running a command using the environment from a- *.env*file (currently Unix only)

## Usage

### Loading at runtime

```
use env;
use Error;
```
### Loading at compile time

The `dotenv!` macro provided by `dotenvy_macro` crate can be used.

Warning: there is an outstanding issue with rust-analyzer ([rust-analyzer #9606](https://github.com/rust-analyzer/rust-analyzer/issues/9606)) related to the `dotenv!` macro

## Minimum supported Rust version

Currently: **1.56.1**

We aim to support the latest 8 rustc versions - approximately 1 year. Increasing
MSRV is *not* considered a semver-breaking change.

## Why does this fork exist?

The original dotenv crate has not been updated since June 26, 2020. Attempts to reach the authors and present maintainer were not successful ([dotenv-rs/dotenv #74](https://github.com/dotenv-rs/dotenv/issues/74)).

This fork intends to serve as the development home for the dotenv implementation in Rust.

## What are the differences from the original?

This repo fixes:

- more helpful errors for `dotenv!`([dotenv-rs/dotenv #57](https://github.com/dotenv-rs/dotenv/pull/57))

It also adds:

- multiline support for environment variable values
- `io::Read`support via- `from_read`- `from_read_iter`
- override support via [`dotenv_override`], [`from_filename_override`], [`from_path_override`] and [`from_read_override`]
- improved docs

For a full list of changes, refer to the [changelog](https://docs.rs/CHANGELOG.md).

## The legend

Legend has it that the Lost Maintainer will return, merging changes from `dotenvy` into `dotenv` with such thrust that all `Cargo.toml`s will lose one keystroke. Only then shall the Rust dotenv crateverse be united in true harmony.

Until then, this repo dutifully carries on the dotenv torch. It is actively maintained. Contributions and PRs are very welcome!

---

# tempfile 3.27.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/tempfile/^3.2

# tempfile

A secure, cross-platform, temporary file library for Rust. In addition to creating temporary files, this library also allows users to securely open multiple independent references to the same temporary file (useful for consumer/producer patterns and surprisingly difficult to implement securely).

## Usage

Minimum required Rust version: 1.63.0

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "3"
```
## Supported Platforms

This crate supports all major operating systems:

- Linux
- Android
- MacOS
- Windows
- FreeBSD (likely other BSDs but we don't have CI for them)
- RedoxOS
- Wasm (build and link only, Wasm doesn't have a filesystem)
- WASI P1 & P2.

However:

- Android, RedoxOS, Wasm, and WASI targets all require the latest stable rust compiler.
- WASI P1/P2 does not define a default temporary directory. You'll need to explicitly call `tempfile::env::override_temp_dir`with a valid directory or temporary file creation will panic on this platform.
- WASI P1/P2 does not have file permissions.
- You *may*need to override the temporary directory in Android as well to point at your application's per-app cache directory.

## Example

```
use File;
use ;
```

---

# diesel_migrations 2.3.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/diesel_migrations/2.3.2

Provides functions for maintaining database schema.

A database migration always provides procedures to update the schema, as well as to revert itself. Diesel's migrations are versioned, and run in order. Diesel also takes care of tracking which migrations have already been run automatically. Your migrations don't need to be idempotent, as Diesel will ensure no migration is run twice unless it has been reverted.

Migrations should be placed in a `/migrations` directory at the root of your project (the same
directory as `Cargo.toml`). When any of these functions are run, Diesel will search for the
migrations directory in the current directory and its parents, stopping when it finds the
directory containing `Cargo.toml`.

Individual migrations should be a folder containing two files, `up.sql` and `down.sql`.
`up.sql` will be used to run the migration, while `down.sql` will be used for reverting it. The
folder itself should have the structure `{version}_{migration_name}`. It is recommended that
you use the timestamp of creation for the version.

Migrations can either be run with the CLI or embedded into the compiled application
and executed with code, for example right after establishing a database connection.
For more information, consult the [`embed_migrations!`] macro.

## Transactions

By default, each migration runs inside its own transaction. This means a failing migration is automatically rolled back, leaving the database in the state it was in before the migration started.

You can disable this behaviour on a per-migration basis. For file-based migrations,
add a `metadata.toml` file to the migration folder with `run_in_transaction = false`.
See [`FileBasedMigrations`] for a full example and an explanation of the
"cannot run inside a transaction block" error that certain database operations produce.

---

# diesel_migrations 1.3.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/diesel_migrations/1.3.0

Provides functions for maintaining database schema.

A database migration always provides procedures to update the schema, as well as to revert itself. Diesel's migrations are versioned, and run in order. Diesel also takes care of tracking which migrations have already been run automatically. Your migrations don't need to be idempotent, as Diesel will ensure no migration is run twice unless it has been reverted.

Migrations should be placed in a `/migrations` directory at the root of your project (the same
directory as `Cargo.toml`). When any of these functions are run, Diesel will search for the
migrations directory in the current directory and its parents, stopping when it finds the
directory containing `Cargo.toml`.

Individual migrations should be a folder containing exactly two files, `up.sql` and `down.sql`.
`up.sql` will be used to run the migration, while `down.sql` will be used for reverting it. The
folder itself should have the structure `{version}_{migration_name}`. It is recommended that
you use the timestamp of creation for the version.

Migrations can either be run with the CLI or embedded into the compiled application
and executed with code, for example right after establishing a database connection.
For more information, consult the [ embed_migrations!](https://docs.rs/macro.embed_migrations.html) macro.

## Example

```
# Directory Structure
- 20151219180527_create_users
- up.sql
- down.sql
- 20160107082941_create_posts
- up.sql
- down.sql
```
```
-- 20151219180527_create_users/up.sql
 (
id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
name VARCHAR NOT NULL,
hair_color VARCHAR
);
```
```
-- 20151219180527_create_users/down.sql
 users;
```
```
-- 20160107082941_create_posts/up.sql
 (
id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
user_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
title VARCHAR NOT NULL,
body TEXT
);
```
```
-- 20160107082941_create_posts/down.sql
 posts;
```

---

# pivx_rpc - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/pivx-rpc/0.3.0/pivx_rpc/

## Expand description

PIVX SDK: typed JSON-RPC client for pivxd with first-class support for shielded (SHIELD/Sapling) balances and transactions.

```
use pivx_rpc::{Auth, PivxClient, ShieldRecipient, ShieldWatcher, WatchOptions};
let client = PivxClient::new(
    "http://127.0.0.1:51473",
    Auth::UserPass { user: "rpcuser".into(), pass: "rpcpass".into() },
)?;
// Watch a shielded address via its viewing key (no spend key needed).
let imported = client.import_sapling_viewing_key("p-view-key...", None, None).await?;
let mut watcher = ShieldWatcher::new(&client, WatchOptions {
    addresses: vec![imported.address],
    ..Default::default()
});
let events = watcher.poll().await?; // first poll primes silently
// Send shielded funds (node wallet holds the keys and builds the proof).
let txid = client
    .shield_send_many(
        pivx_rpc::FromAddress::AnyShield,
        &[ShieldRecipient::new("ps1...", 1.5).with_memo("hello")],
    )
    .await?;
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Block](https://docs.rs/struct.BlockHeader.html)- Header
- Verbose block header (`getblockheader`, verbose=true). For the raw serialized header use`get_block`with verbosity 0.
- [Blockchain](https://docs.rs/struct.BlockchainInfo.html)- Info
- [Chain](https://docs.rs/struct.ChainTip.html)- Tip
- One entry of `getchaintips`.
- [Decoded](https://docs.rs/struct.DecodedTransaction.html)- Transaction
- Decoded transaction (`decoderawtransaction`, verbose`getrawtransaction`).
- [Imported](https://docs.rs/struct.ImportedSaplingKey.html)- Sapling - Key
- Result of `importsaplingkey`/`importsaplingviewingkey`.
- [List](https://docs.rs/struct.ListSinceBlock.html)- Since - Block
- Result of `list_since_block`. PIVX omits the`removed`array.
- [List](https://docs.rs/struct.ListTransaction.html)- Transaction
- Element of `list_transactions`/`list_since_block`(long form: the listtransactions fields plus the embedded wallet-tx fields).
- [Pivx](https://docs.rs/struct.PivxClient.html)- Client
- Async JSON-RPC client for a pivxd node.
- [PrevTx](https://docs.rs/struct.PrevTx.html)
- Previous-output spec for `sign_raw_transaction`.
- [Received](https://docs.rs/struct.ReceivedShieldNote.html)- Shield - Note
- Received note, as returned by `listreceivedbyshieldaddress`.
- [Script](https://docs.rs/struct.ScriptPubKey.html)- PubKey
- Script of a transaction output (`gettxout`, decoded-tx vout).
- [Script](https://docs.rs/struct.ScriptSig.html)- Sig
- [Shield](https://docs.rs/struct.ShieldNote.html)- Note
- Unspent shielded note, as returned by `listshieldunspent`.
- [Shield](https://docs.rs/struct.ShieldPoolValue.html)- Pool - Value
- [Shield](https://docs.rs/struct.ShieldRecipient.html)- Recipient
- Recipient entry for `shieldsendmany`/`rawshieldsendmany`.
- [Shield](https://docs.rs/struct.ShieldTxOutput.html)- TxOutput
- [Shield](https://docs.rs/struct.ShieldTxSpend.html)- TxSpend
- [Shield](https://docs.rs/struct.ShieldTxView.html)- TxView
- Decrypted view of a shielded transaction (`viewshieldtransaction`).
- [Shield](https://docs.rs/struct.ShieldWatcher.html)- Watcher
- Polls the node and reports `ShieldEvent`
- [Sign](https://docs.rs/struct.SignError.html)- Error
- [Sign](https://docs.rs/struct.SignRawTransactionResult.html)- RawTransaction - Result
- Result of `sign_raw_transaction`.
- [Transaction](https://docs.rs/struct.Transaction.html)
- Wallet’s record of a transaction (`gettransaction`).
- [Transaction](https://docs.rs/struct.TransactionDetail.html)- Detail
- Short detail element embedded in `gettransaction`.
- [TxInput](https://docs.rs/struct.TxInput.html)
- Input spec for `create_raw_transaction`.
- [TxOut](https://docs.rs/struct.TxOut.html)
- Unspent output details (`gettxout`); the call returns`None`when spent or not found.
- [Unspent](https://docs.rs/struct.Unspent.html)
- [Validate](https://docs.rs/struct.ValidateAddress.html)- Address
- Result of `validate_address`. Only`isvalid`is guaranteed; the rest depend on validity and address type (transparent vs shield).
- [Vin](https://docs.rs/struct.Vin.html)
- Input of a decoded transaction. Coinbase inputs carry `coinbase`; every other input carries`txid`/`vout`/`script_sig`.
- [Vout](https://docs.rs/struct.Vout.html)
- Output of a decoded transaction.
- [Wallet](https://docs.rs/struct.WalletInfo.html)- Info
- [Watch](https://docs.rs/struct.WatchOptions.html)- Options
- Options for `ShieldWatcher`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Auth](https://docs.rs/enum.Auth.html)
- Authentication for the node’s RPC interface.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html)
- [From](https://docs.rs/enum.FromAddress.html)- Address
- Source for `shieldsendmany`: an address or a selector.
- [Shield](https://docs.rs/enum.ShieldEvent.html)- Event
- Change observed in the wallet’s shielded note set.

# odcs - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/odcs/0.9.1/odcs/

## Expand description

Reference implementation of the Open Data Contract Standard (ODCS).

This is a **reference implementation** — not the normative ODCS specification.
The upstream standard is maintained at
[bitol-io/open-data-contract-standard](https://github.com/bitol-io/open-data-contract-standard).

[§](https://docs.rs#user-documentation)User documentation

[§](https://docs.rs#pipeline)Pipeline

`ODCS Document → Parser → Canonical Object Model → Validator → Diagnostics`[§](https://docs.rs#stable-api)Stable API

Use root re-exports only (`parse`, `validate`, `parse_and_validate`, `DataContract`,
`ContractSet`, `Registry`, `diff`, …). Internal modules (`parser`, `validation`, `model`, …)
are `#[doc(hidden)]` and not semver-stable. See the
[public API guide](https://odcs.readthedocs.io/en/latest/implementation/public-api.md).

[§](https://docs.rs#error-handling)Error handling

- `parse`- `parse_and_validate`- `DiagnosticReport`- `ParseResult`
- `parse_file`- `DataContract::from_file`- `miette::Result`for I/O errors
- `ParseResult::into_contract`- `parse_strict`- `Result<DataContract, DiagnosticReport>`after parse and validation

Match on diagnostic [ codes](https://docs.rs/codes/index.html) and

`object_ref`, not message text.[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use odcs::{parse, validate, DocumentFormat};
let yaml = br#"
version: "1.0.0"
apiVersion: "v3.1.0"
kind: "DataContract"
id: "example"
status: "draft"
"#;
let result = parse(yaml, DocumentFormat::Yaml);
let contract = result.contract.expect("parse succeeded");
let report = validate(&contract);
assert!(report.is_valid());
```
## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use compatibility::`- [diff](https://docs.rs/compatibility/fn.diff.html);

# fakecloud_resource_groups - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/fakecloud-resource-groups/0.31.0/fakecloud_resource_groups/

## Expand description

AWS Resource Groups (`resource-groups`) restJson1 service for fakecloud.

Batch 1: the full 23-operation control plane from the AWS Smithy model –
group lifecycle (Create/Get/Update/Delete/ListGroups), resource queries
(GetGroupQuery/UpdateGroupQuery), explicit membership
(GroupResources/UngroupResources/ListGroupResources), search
(SearchResources), group configuration (Get/PutGroupConfiguration), tagging
(Tag/Untag/GetTags), account settings (Get/UpdateAccountSettings), grouping
statuses (ListGroupingStatuses), and tag-sync tasks
(Start/Get/List/CancelTagSyncTask). Every operation is backed by real,
account-partitioned, persisted state with AWS-shaped
`arn:aws:resource-groups:...:group/<name>/<id>` ARNs.

Query-based membership resolution (evaluating a `TAG_FILTERS_1_0` /
`CLOUDFORMATION_STACK_1_0` query against live resources) depends on the
cross-service tag index that ships with the Resource Groups Tagging API
batch; until then a query-based group resolves to its explicitly associated
members. Explicit `GroupResources` membership is fully real now.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use service::`- [ResourceGroupsService](https://docs.rs/service/struct.ResourceGroupsService.html);
- `pub use state::`- [ResourceGroupsState](https://docs.rs/state/struct.ResourceGroupsState.html);
- `pub use state::`- [RESOURCE_GROUPS_SNAPSHOT_SCHEMA_VERSION](https://docs.rs/state/constant.RESOURCE_GROUPS_SNAPSHOT_SCHEMA_VERSION.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [persistence](https://docs.rs/persistence/index.html)
- Snapshot save/load for Resource Groups state.
- [service](https://docs.rs/service/index.html)
- Resource Groups restJson1 dispatch + operation handlers.
- [state](https://docs.rs/state/index.html)
- Account-partitioned, serializable state for AWS Resource Groups.

# sim_lib_logic - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-lib-logic/0.1.0-rc.1/sim_lib_logic/

## Expand description

Logic behavior for the SIM runtime: clauses, unification, and queries.

The kernel defines the `Shape`, eval-policy, and codec contracts; this crate
supplies the concrete logic organ (a clause database, unifier, constraint
solving, and a query/stream surface).

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use policy::`- [LogicPolicy](https://docs.rs/policy/struct.LogicPolicy.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [builtins](https://docs.rs/builtins/index.html)
- Browseable logic builtin bindings.
- [policy](https://docs.rs/policy/index.html)
- Eval-policy adapter for running logic queries through a `sim_kernel::Cx`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Clause](https://docs.rs/struct.Clause.html)
- A parsed logic clause: a head goal plus an optional list of body goals.
- [Clause](https://docs.rs/struct.ClauseId.html)- Id
- Stable identifier assigned to a clause when it is added to a database.
- [Logic](https://docs.rs/struct.LogicConfig.html)- Config
- Aggregate tuning for the logic organ, threaded through every query.
- [LogicDb](https://docs.rs/struct.LogicDb.html)
- An indexed store of logic `Clause`
- [Logic](https://docs.rs/struct.LogicEnv.html)- Env
- A unification substitution: bindings from logic variables to terms.
- [Logic](https://docs.rs/struct.LogicLib.html)- Lib
- The loadable logic organ: shapes, functions, and database/config state.
- [Logic](https://docs.rs/struct.LogicLimits.html)- Limits
- Resource ceilings that bound a single logic query.
- [Logic](https://docs.rs/struct.LogicQuery.html)- Query
- A goal paired with the `LogicConfig`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Occurs](https://docs.rs/enum.OccursCheck.html)- Check
- Whether the unifier runs the occurs check when binding a variable.
- [Search](https://docs.rs/enum.SearchStrategy.html)- Strategy
- Order in which the resolver explores pending goal states.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [install_](https://docs.rs/fn.install_logic_lib.html)- logic_ - lib
- Installs the `LogicLib``cx`, idempotently.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_clause_expr.html)- clause_ - expr
- Parses a `(fact head)`or`(rule head body)`expression into a`Clause`
- [query](https://docs.rs/fn.query.html)
- Resolves `goal`against`db`and returns the answers as a logic stream.
- [query_](https://docs.rs/fn.query_all.html)- all
- Resolves `goal`against`db`and returns all answers up to`limit`.
- [query_](https://docs.rs/fn.query_all_with_builtins.html)- all_ - with_ - builtins
- Resolves `goal`with an explicit builtin table.
- [realize_](https://docs.rs/fn.realize_logic.html)- logic
- Resolves `goal`against the installed logic database and returns the result.
- [unify_](https://docs.rs/fn.unify_exprs.html)- exprs
- Unifies two expressions and reports the result as a kernel `ShapeMatch`.

# yatrosci_sparse - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yatrosci-sparse/0.1.0/yatrosci_sparse/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#scirs-sparse-matrices)SciRS Sparse Matrices

Sparse matrix data structures and algorithms for scientific computing,
providing functionality equivalent to `scipy.sparse`.

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

This crate provides:

- Sparse matrix formats: CSR, CSC, COO, DOK, LIL, DIA, BSR
- Sparse matrix construction utilities
- Sparse linear algebra operations
- Format conversion between sparse representations
- Sparse-dense and sparse-sparse operations

[§](https://docs.rs#sparse-formats)Sparse Formats

| Format | Description | Best For |
|---|---|---|
| CSR | Compressed Sparse Row | Row slicing, matrix-vector products |
| CSC | Compressed Sparse Column | Column slicing, arithmetic operations |
| COO | Coordinate Format | Incremental construction |
| DOK | Dictionary of Keys | Random access insertion |
| LIL | List of Lists | Row-wise construction |
| DIA | Diagonal Format | Diagonal/banded matrices |
| BSR | Block Sparse Row | Block-structured matrices |

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use yatrosci_sparse::{CsrMatrix, CooMatrix};
use ndarray::array;
// Create COO matrix and convert to CSR
let mut coo = CooMatrix::<f64>::new(3, 3);
coo.push(0, 0, 1.0);
coo.push(1, 1, 2.0);
coo.push(2, 2, 3.0);
let csr = coo.to_csr();
```

- `pub use construct::`- [hstack](https://docs.rs/construct/fn.hstack.html);

- `pub use construct::`- [vstack](https://docs.rs/construct/fn.vstack.html);

# fakecloud_rds_data - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/fakecloud-rds-data/0.31.0/fakecloud_rds_data/

## Expand description

AWS RDS Data API (`rds-data`) restJson1 service for fakecloud.

Batch 1: vendored Smithy model + crate scaffold + restJson1 routing for the
Data API operations + a real `ExecuteStatement` that resolves the
`resourceArn` to a fakecloud-managed RDS container DB and runs the SQL for
real over `tokio-postgres` / `mysql_async`, returning AWS-shaped typed
`Field` records + `columnMetadata`. This is the wedge: rival emulators serve
canned rows or return `{}` for binary columns; fakecloud runs genuine SQL on
a real engine. Transactions + `BatchExecuteStatement` land in later batches;
unimplemented operations return a faithful `BadRequestException`/not-yet
error rather than a fake success.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use service::`- [RdsDataService](https://docs.rs/service/struct.RdsDataService.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [service](https://docs.rs/service/index.html)
- RDS Data API (`rds-data`) restJson1 dispatch + real SQL execution.

# claim_ledger - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/claim-ledger/0.1.1/claim_ledger/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#claim-ledger)claim-ledger

Deterministic, local-first claim/evidence/provenance ledger.

Creates receipts for all material operations.

[§](https://docs.rs#core-concepts)Core Concepts

- **Claim**: A source-spanned atomic assertion extracted from a document.
- **Evidence Bundle**: A collection of evidence links supporting a claim.
- **Support Judgment**: A scoped support state assigned to a claim via an evidence bundle.
- **Support Admission**: An operator-admitted or fixture-admitted upgrade to a support judgment.
- **Contradiction Record**: A detected conflict between two claims with a resolution lifecycle.
- **Claim Ledger**: An append-only, hash-chained ledger of claim events and support states.
- **Export Receipt**: A binding receipt digest for any material output operation.

[§](https://docs.rs#crate-architecture)Crate Architecture

# pyde_host - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/pyde-host/0.1.0-alpha.7/pyde_host/

## Expand description

Canonical Pyde host-function declarations for `wasm32` contracts.

Re-exports the full `pyde::*` ABI a Rust contract can call into
— every host fn declared in [HOST_FN_ABI_SPEC §7](https://book.pyde.network/companion/HOST_FN_ABI_SPEC).

[§](https://docs.rs#pointer-convention)Pointer convention

All `*const u8` / `*mut u8` parameters are 32-bit offsets into
linear memory (`wasm32-unknown-unknown` makes pointers 4 bytes).
Multi-byte integers cross the boundary in little-endian (matching
WASM’s native byte order) unless the spec explicitly says
otherwise — see HOST_FN_ABI_SPEC §3.2.

[§](https://docs.rs#dead-code-elimination)Dead-code elimination

Unused declarations are stripped by the linker’s DCE — your
final `.wasm` only imports what you actually call. Safe to
depend on this crate even if you only use a handful of host fns.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [call](https://docs.rs/call/index.html)
- Cross-contract calls with `Result<T, CallError>`ergonomics.
- [calldata](https://docs.rs/calldata/index.html)
- Calldata helpers — wraps the size-probe + read pattern.
- [ctx](https://docs.rs/ctx/index.html)
- Execution + transaction context.
- [hash](https://docs.rs/hash/index.html)
- Hashing primitives.
- [raw](https://docs.rs/raw/index.html)
- Raw FFI host-function declarations — the chain-facing ABI as a
flat `extern "C"`surface. Every Pyde host function in`HOST_FN_ABI_SPEC.md`lives here.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [declare_](https://docs.rs/macro.declare_events.html)- events
- `pyde::declare_events!()`— reads- `otigen.toml`at compile time and emits a- `mod events`with one typed struct +- `emit()`impl per declared event. Author writes
- [declare_](https://docs.rs/macro.declare_storage.html)- storage
- `pyde::declare_storage!()`— reads- `otigen.toml`at compile time and emits a- `mod storage`with one typed accessor per declared field. Author writes

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [consume_](https://docs.rs/fn.consume_gas.html)- gas
- Charge `amount`units of gas explicitly. Useful for surfacing off-fuel computation cost (synchronous loops bounded by external data) in receipts.
- [emit_](https://docs.rs/fn.emit_event.html)- event
- Emit a log event from the current call frame.
- [return_](https://docs.rs/fn.return_.html)
- Return `data`from the current call frame. The bytes flow into the receipt’s`return_data`for top-level calls, and into the caller’s return slot for`cross_call`. Does not return.
- [revert](https://docs.rs/fn.revert.html)
- Revert the current call frame with a UTF-8 message.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Address](https://docs.rs/type.Address.html)
- 32-byte Pyde address. Same byte layout as the chain’s
`pyde_engine_types::Address`but kept as a thin alias here so contracts don’t pull the heavy engine-types crate in.
- [Hash32](https://docs.rs/type.Hash32.html)
- 32-byte hash digest. Used for content hashes, pubkey-derived
identifiers, and any other fixed 32-byte value that isn’t an
account address. `bytes32`in`otigen.toml`resolves to this (Solidity-compat alias).

## Attribute Macros[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)

- [entry](https://docs.rs/attr.entry.html)
- `#[pyde::entry]`— wraps a function in the- `() -> ()`WASM shim required by Pyde’s entry-point ABI. Re-exported from- `pyde-entry-macros`so contract authors only need one crate dependency to write idiomatic Pyde contracts.

# pyde_events_macros - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/pyde-events-macros/0.1.0-alpha.7/pyde_events_macros/

## Expand description

`pyde-events-macros` — backing crate for `pyde::declare_events!()`.

Re-exported from `pyde-host`; contracts never depend on this crate
directly. The function-like macro reads `otigen.toml` at compile
time, parses every `[events.NAME]` block, computes the canonical
topic-0 hash (`Blake3(signature)`) for each, and emits a typed
struct + `emit()` impl under `mod events`. Authors write

and the macro expands into the equivalent
`pyde::emit_event(&[TOPIC0, from, to], &borsh::to_vec(&amount).unwrap())`
call — same wire bytes as a hand-rolled emission, but the topic-0
hash + indexed-topic layout + data encoding are all derived from
`otigen.toml` so a typo at any layer is a compile error.

[§](https://docs.rs#expansion-shape)Expansion shape

For an `otigen.toml` `[events.Transfer]` block like

```
[events.Transfer]
signature = "Transfer(address,address,uint128)"
fields = [
    { name = "from",   type = "address",  indexed = true },
    { name = "to",     type = "address",  indexed = true },
    { name = "amount", type = "uint128" },
]
```
the macro emits roughly

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
pub mod events {
    pub struct Transfer {
        pub from: ::pyde_host::Address,
        pub to: ::pyde_host::Address,
        pub amount: u128,
    }
    impl Transfer {
        pub const TOPIC_0: ::pyde_host::Hash32 = [0x71, 0xfb, /* ... */];
        pub fn emit(&self) {
            let topics = [Self::TOPIC_0, self.from, self.to];
            let data = self.amount.to_le_bytes();
            ::pyde_host::emit_event(&topics, &data);
        }
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#restrictions-in-v1)Restrictions in v1

- Indexed fields must be `address`,`hash32`, or`bytes32`(the 32-byte fixed-width types). Hashing a variable-width indexed value to fit it into a 32-byte topic is a separate convention the chain doesn’t yet pick a side on.
- Non-indexed fields support all primitives (`u8`..`u128`,`i8`..`i128`,`bool`,`address`,`hash32`,`bytes32`,`bytes`,`string`). Multiple non-indexed fields are encoded as a borsh tuple in declaration order.
- Max 4 topics (chain limit, see `HOST_FN_ABI_SPEC`§7.5). With topic[0] reserved for the signature hash, that leaves 3 indexed fields max per event.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [declare_](https://docs.rs/macro.declare_events.html)- events
- `declare_events!()`— read otigen.toml at compile time, emit- `mod events`. Takes no arguments.

# fakecloud_dsql - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/fakecloud-dsql/0.31.0/fakecloud_dsql/

## Expand description

AWS Aurora DSQL (`dsql`) restJson1 control-plane service for fakecloud.

Batch 1: the full 16-operation control plane from the AWS Smithy model –
cluster lifecycle (Create/Get/Update/Delete/ListClusters), resource-based
cluster policies (Put/Get/DeleteClusterPolicy), change streams
(Create/Get/Delete/ListStreams), the VPC endpoint service-name lookup, and
tagging (Tag/Untag/ListTagsForResource). Every operation is backed by real,
account-partitioned, persisted state with AWS-shaped identifiers (26-char
lowercase cluster ids, `arn:aws:dsql:...:cluster/<id>` ARNs), an async
CREATING -> ACTIVE / DELETING -> DELETED lifecycle, `clientToken`
idempotency, deletion-protection enforcement, and multi-region property
round-tripping.

The Postgres-compatible data plane (a real container the cluster endpoint resolves to, reachable with an IAM-derived connection token) lands in a follow-up batch; this batch establishes the control plane and full non-code surface. Unimplemented behavior returns a faithful modeled error, never a stub success.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use service::`- [DsqlService](https://docs.rs/service/struct.DsqlService.html);
- `pub use state::`- [DsqlState](https://docs.rs/state/struct.DsqlState.html);
- `pub use state::`- [DSQL_SNAPSHOT_SCHEMA_VERSION](https://docs.rs/state/constant.DSQL_SNAPSHOT_SCHEMA_VERSION.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [persistence](https://docs.rs/persistence/index.html)
- Snapshot save/load helpers for the DSQL control-plane state.
- [service](https://docs.rs/service/index.html)
- Aurora DSQL restJson1 control-plane dispatch and operation handlers.
- [state](https://docs.rs/state/index.html)
- Account-partitioned, serializable state for the Aurora DSQL control plane.
- [ticker](https://docs.rs/ticker/index.html)
- Background lifecycle advancement for DSQL clusters and streams.

# diesel_migrations - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/diesel_migrations/2.3.2/aarch64-apple-darwin/diesel_migrations/

## Expand description

Provides functions for maintaining database schema.

A database migration always provides procedures to update the schema, as well as to revert itself. Diesel’s migrations are versioned, and run in order. Diesel also takes care of tracking which migrations have already been run automatically. Your migrations don’t need to be idempotent, as Diesel will ensure no migration is run twice unless it has been reverted.

Migrations should be placed in a `/migrations` directory at the root of your project (the same
directory as `Cargo.toml`). When any of these functions are run, Diesel will search for the
migrations directory in the current directory and its parents, stopping when it finds the
directory containing `Cargo.toml`.

Individual migrations should be a folder containing two files, `up.sql` and `down.sql`.
`up.sql` will be used to run the migration, while `down.sql` will be used for reverting it. The
folder itself should have the structure `{version}_{migration_name}`. It is recommended that
you use the timestamp of creation for the version.

Migrations can either be run with the CLI or embedded into the compiled application
and executed with code, for example right after establishing a database connection.
For more information, consult the [ embed_migrations!](https://docs.rs/macro.embed_migrations.html) macro.

[§](https://docs.rs#transactions)Transactions

By default, each migration runs inside its own transaction. This means a failing migration is automatically rolled back, leaving the database in the state it was in before the migration started.

You can disable this behaviour on a per-migration basis. For file-based migrations,
add a `metadata.toml` file to the migration folder with `run_in_transaction = false`.
See [ FileBasedMigrations](https://docs.rs/struct.FileBasedMigrations.html) for a full example and an explanation of the
“cannot run inside a transaction block” error that certain database operations produce.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [embed_](https://docs.rs/macro.embed_migrations.html)- migrations
- This macro will read your migrations at compile time, and create a constant value containing an embedded list of all your migrations as available at compile time. This is useful if you would like to use Diesel’s migration infrastructure, but want to ship a single executable file (such as for embedded applications). It can also be used to apply migrations to an in memory database (Diesel does this for its own test suite).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Embedded](https://docs.rs/struct.EmbeddedMigrations.html)- Migrations
- A migration source that embeds migrations into the final binary
- [File](https://docs.rs/struct.FileBasedMigrations.html)- Based - Migrations
- A migration source based on a migration directory in the file system
- [Harness](https://docs.rs/struct.HarnessWithOutput.html)- With - Output
- A migration harness that writes messages into some output for each applied/reverted migration

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Migration](https://docs.rs/trait.MigrationHarness.html)- Harness
- A migration harness is an entity which applies migration to an existing database

# diesel - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/diesel/~2.3.0/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#diesel)Diesel

Diesel is an ORM and query builder designed to reduce the boilerplate for database interactions.
If this is your first time reading this documentation,
we recommend you start with the [getting started guide](https://diesel.rs/guides/getting-started/).
We also have [many other long form guides](https://diesel.rs/guides).

[§](https://docs.rs#where-to-find-things)Where to find things

[§](https://docs.rs#declaring-your-schema)Declaring your schema

For Diesel to validate your queries at compile time
it requires you to specify your schema in your code,
which you can do with [the  table! macro](https://docs.rs/macro.table.html).

`diesel print-schema` can be used
to automatically generate these macro calls
(by connecting to your database and querying its schema).[§](https://docs.rs#getting-started)Getting started

Queries usually start from either a table, or a function like [ update](https://docs.rs/fn.update.html).
Those functions can be found

[here](https://docs.rs#functions).

Diesel provides a [ prelude module](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html),
which exports most of the typically used traits and types.
We are conservative about what goes in this module,
and avoid anything which has a generic name.
Files which use Diesel are expected to have

`use diesel::prelude::*;`.[§](https://docs.rs#constructing-a-query)Constructing a query

The tools the query builder gives you can be put into these three categories:

- “Query builder methods” are things that map to portions of a whole query
(such as `ORDER`and`WHERE`). These methods usually have the same name as the SQL they map to, except for`WHERE`which is called`filter`in Diesel (To not conflict with the Rust keyword). These methods live in[the](https://docs.rs/query_dsl/index.html).`query_dsl`module
- “Expression methods” are things you would call on columns
or other individual values.
These methods live in [the](https://docs.rs/expression_methods/index.html)You can often find these by thinking “what would this be called” if it were a method and typing that into the search bar (e.g.`expression_methods`module`LIKE`is called`like`in Diesel). Most operators are named based on the Rust function which maps to that operator in`std::ops``==`is called`.eq`, and`!=`is called`.ne`).
- “Bare functions” are normal SQL functions
such as `sum`. They live in[the](https://docs.rs/dsl/index.html). Diesel only supports a very small number of these functions. You can declare additional functions you want to use with`dsl`module[the](https://docs.rs/prelude/macro.define_sql_function.html).`define_sql_function!`macro

[§](https://docs.rs#serializing-and-deserializing)Serializing and Deserializing

Types which represent the result of a SQL query implement
a trait called [ Queryable](https://docs.rs/deserialize/trait.Queryable.html).

Diesel maps “Rust types” (e.g. `i32`) to and from “SQL types”
(e.g. [ diesel::sql_types::Integer](https://docs.rs/sql_types/struct.Integer.html)).
You can find all the types supported by Diesel in

[the](https://docs.rs/sql_types/index.html). These types are only used to represent a SQL type. You should never put them on your

`sql_types` module`Queryable` structs.To find all the Rust types which can be used with a given SQL type, see the documentation for that SQL type.

To find all the SQL types which can be used with a Rust type,
go to the docs for either [ ToSql](https://docs.rs/serialize/trait.ToSql.html) or

[, go to the “Implementors” section, and find the Rust type you want to use.](https://docs.rs/deserialize/trait.FromSql.html)

`FromSql`[§](https://docs.rs#how-to-read-diesels-compile-time-error-messages)How to read diesels compile time error messages

Diesel is known for generating large complicated looking errors. Usually
most of these error messages can be broken down easily. The following
section tries to give an overview of common error messages and how to read them.
As a general note it’s always useful to read the complete error message as emitted
by rustc, including the `required because of …` part of the message.
Your IDE might hide important parts!

The following error messages are common:

- `the trait bound (diesel::sql_types::Integer, …, diesel::sql_types::Text): load_dsl::private::CompatibleType<YourModel, Pg> is not satisfied`while trying to execute a query: This error indicates a mismatch between what your query returns and what your model struct expects the query to return. The fields need to match in terms of field order, field type and field count. If you are sure that everything matches, double check the enabled diesel features (for support for types from other crates) and double check (via- `cargo tree`) that there is only one version of such a shared crate in your dependency tree. Consider using- `#[derive(Selectable)]`- `#[diesel(check_for_backend(diesel::pg::Pg))]`to improve the generated error message.
- `the trait bound i32: diesel::Expression is not satisfied`in the context of- `Insertable`model structs: This error indicates a type mismatch between the field you are trying to insert into the database and the actual database type. These error messages contain a line like- `= note: required for i32 to implement AsExpression<diesel::sql_types::Text>`that show both the provided rust side type (- `i32`in that case) and the expected database side type (- `Text`in that case).
- `the trait bound i32: AppearsOnTable<users::table> is not satisfied`in the context of- `AsChangeset`model structs: This error indicates a type mismatch between the field you are trying to update and the actual database type. Double check your type mapping.
- `the trait bound SomeLargeType: QueryFragment<Sqlite, SomeMarkerType> is not satisfied`while trying to execute a query. This error message indicates that a given query is not supported by your backend. This usually means that you are trying to use SQL features from one SQL dialect on a different database system. Double check your query that everything required is supported by the selected backend. If that’s the case double check that the relevant feature flags are enabled (for example,- `returning_clauses_for_sqlite_3_35`for enabling support for returning clauses in newer sqlite versions)
- `the trait bound posts::title: SelectableExpression<users::table> is not satisfied`while executing a query: This error message indicates that you’re trying to select a field from a table that does not appear in your from clause. If your query joins the relevant table via- `left_join`- `.nullable()`

[§](https://docs.rs#getting-help)Getting help

If you run into problems, Diesel has an active community.
Open a new [discussion](https://github.com/diesel-rs/diesel/discussions/categories/q-a) thread at diesel github repository
and we will try to help you

[§](https://docs.rs#crate-feature-flags)Crate feature flags

The following feature flags are considered to be part of diesels public
API. Any feature flag that is not listed here is **not** considered to
be part of the public API and can disappear at any point in time:

- `sqlite`: This feature enables the diesel sqlite backend. Enabling this feature requires per default a compatible copy of- `libsqlite3`for your target architecture. Alternatively, you can add- `libsqlite3-sys`with the- `bundled`feature as a dependency to your crate so SQLite will be bundled:- `[dependencies] libsqlite3-sys = { version = "0.29", features = ["bundled"] }`
- `postgres`: This feature enables the diesel postgres backend. This features implies- `postgres_backend`Enabling this feature requires a compatible copy of- `libpq`for your target architecture. Alternatively, you can add- `pq-sys`with the- `bundled`feature as a dependency to your crate so libpq will be bundled:- `[dependencies] pq-sys = { version = "0.6", features = ["bundled"] } openssl-sys = { version = "0.9.100", features = ["vendored"] }`
- `mysql`: This feature enables the diesel mysql backend. This feature implies- `mysql_backend`. Enabling this feature requires a compatible copy of- `libmysqlclient`for your target architecture. Alternatively, you can add- `mysqlclient-sys`with the- `bundled`feature as a dependency to your crate so libmysqlclient will be bundled:- `[dependencies] mysqlclient-sys = { version = "0.5", features = ["bundled"] } openssl-sys = { version = "0.9.100", features = ["vendored"] }`
- `postgres_backend`: This feature enables those parts of diesels postgres backend, that are not dependent on- `libpq`. Diesel does not provide any connection implementation with only this feature enabled. This feature can be used to implement a custom implementation of diesels- `Connection`trait for the postgres backend outside of diesel itself, while reusing the existing query dsl extensions for the postgres backend
- `mysql_backend`: This feature enables those parts of diesels mysql backend, that are not dependent on- `libmysqlclient`. Diesel does not provide any connection implementation with only this feature enabled. This feature can be used to implement a custom implementation of diesels- `Connection`trait for the mysql backend outside of diesel itself, while reusing the existing query dsl extensions for the mysql backend
- `returning_clauses_for_sqlite_3_35`: This feature enables support for- `RETURNING`clauses in the sqlite backend. Enabling this feature requires sqlite 3.35.0 or newer.
- `32-column-tables`: This feature enables support for tables with up to 32 columns. This feature is enabled by default. Consider disabling this feature if you write a library crate providing general extensions for diesel or if you do not need to support tables with more than 16 columns and you want to minimize your compile times.
- `64-column-tables`: This feature enables support for tables with up to 64 columns. It implies the- `32-column-tables`feature. Enabling this feature will increase your compile times.
- `128-column-tables`: This feature enables support for tables with up to 128 columns. It implies the- `64-column-tables`feature. Enabling this feature will increase your compile times significantly.
- `i-implement-a-third-party-backend-and-opt-into-breaking-changes`: This feature opens up some otherwise private API, that can be useful to implement a third party- `Backend`- `Connection`- **Do not use this feature for any other usecase**. By enabling this feature you explicitly opt out diesel stability guarantees. We explicitly reserve us the right to break API’s exported under this feature flag in any upcoming minor version release. If you publish a crate depending on this feature flag consider to restrict the supported diesel version to the currently released minor version.
- `serde_json`: This feature flag enables support for (de)serializing json values from the database using types provided by- `serde_json`.
- `chrono`: This feature flags enables support for (de)serializing date/time values from the database using types provided by- `chrono`
- `uuid`: This feature flag enables support for (de)serializing uuid values from the database using types provided by- `uuid`
- `network-address`: This feature flag enables support for (de)serializing IP values from the database using types provided by- `ipnetwork`.
- `ipnet-address`: This feature flag enables support for (de)serializing IP values from the database using types provided by- `ipnet`.
- `numeric`: This feature flag enables support for (de)serializing numeric values from the database using types provided by- `bigdecimal`
- `r2d2`: This feature flag enables support for the- `r2d2`connection pool implementation.
- `extras`: This feature enables the feature flagged support for any third party crate. This implies the following feature flags:- `serde_json`,- `chrono`,- `uuid`,- `network-address`,- `numeric`,- `r2d2`
- `with-deprecated`: This feature enables items marked as- `#[deprecated]`. It is enabled by default. disabling this feature explicitly opts out diesels stability guarantee.
- `without-deprecated`: This feature disables any item marked as- `#[deprecated]`. Enabling this feature explicitly opts out the stability guarantee given by diesel. This feature overrides the- `with-deprecated`. Note that this may also remove items that are not shown as- `#[deprecated]`in our documentation, due to various bugs in rustdoc. It can be used to check if you depend on any such hidden- `#[deprecated]`item.

By default the following features are enabled:

- `with-deprecated`
- `32-column-tables`

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [associations](https://docs.rs/associations/index.html)
- Traits related to relationships between multiple tables.
- [backend](https://docs.rs/backend/index.html)
- Types which represent various database backends
- [connection](https://docs.rs/connection/index.html)
- Types related to database connections
- [data_](https://docs.rs/data_types/index.html)- types
- Structs to represent the primitive equivalent of SQL types where there is no existing Rust primitive, or where using it would be confusing (such as date and time types). This module will re-export all backend specific data structures when compiled against that backend.
- [deserialize](https://docs.rs/deserialize/index.html)
- Types and traits related to deserializing values from the database
- [dsl](https://docs.rs/dsl/index.html)
- Includes various helper types and bare functions which are named too generically to be included in prelude, but are often used when using Diesel.
- [expression](https://docs.rs/expression/index.html)
- AST types representing various typed SQL expressions.
- [expression_](https://docs.rs/expression_methods/index.html)- methods
- Adds various methods to construct new expressions. These traits are exported by default, and implemented automatically.
- [helper_](https://docs.rs/helper_types/index.html)- types
- Provide helper types for concisely writing the return type of functions. As with iterators, it is unfortunately difficult to return a partially constructed query without exposing the exact implementation of the function. Without higher kinded types, these various DSLs can’t be combined into a single trait for boxing purposes.
- [migration](https://docs.rs/migration/index.html)
- Representation of migrations
- [mysql](https://docs.rs/mysql/index.html)- `mysql_backend`
- Provides types and functions related to working with MySQL
- [pg](https://docs.rs/pg/index.html)- `postgres_backend`
- Provides types and functions related to working with PostgreSQL
- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- Re-exports important traits and types. Meant to be glob imported when using Diesel.
- [query_](https://docs.rs/query_builder/index.html)- builder
- Contains traits responsible for the actual construction of SQL statements
- [query_](https://docs.rs/query_dsl/index.html)- dsl
- Traits that construct SELECT statements
- [query_](https://docs.rs/query_source/index.html)- source
- Types related to describing schema, and interactions between tables.
- [r2d2](https://docs.rs/r2d2/index.html)- `r2d2`
- Connection pooling via r2d2.
- [result](https://docs.rs/result/index.html)
- Errors, type aliases, and functions related to working with `Result`.
- [row](https://docs.rs/row/index.html)
- Contains the `Row`trait
- [serialize](https://docs.rs/serialize/index.html)
- Types and traits related to serializing values for the database
- [sql_](https://docs.rs/sql_types/index.html)- types
- Types which represent a SQL data type.
- [sqlite](https://docs.rs/sqlite/index.html)- `sqlite`
- Provides types and functions related to working with SQLite
- [upsert](https://docs.rs/upsert/index.html)
- Types and functions related to PG’s and Sqlite’s `ON CONFLICT`clause

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [alias](https://docs.rs/macro.alias.html)
- Declare a new alias for a table
- [allow_](https://docs.rs/macro.allow_columns_to_appear_in_same_group_by_clause.html)- columns_ - to_ - appear_ - in_ - same_ - group_ - by_ - clause
- Allow two or more columns which are otherwise unrelated to be used together in a group by clause.
- [allow_](https://docs.rs/macro.allow_tables_to_appear_in_same_query.html)- tables_ - to_ - appear_ - in_ - same_ - query
- Allow two or more tables which are otherwise unrelated to be used together in a query.
- [infix_](https://docs.rs/macro.infix_operator.html)- operator
- Useful for libraries adding support for new SQL types. Apps should never need to call this.
- [joinable](https://docs.rs/macro.joinable.html)
- Allow two tables to be referenced in a join query without providing an
explicit `ON`clause.
- [numeric_](https://docs.rs/macro.numeric_expr.html)- expr
- Indicates that an expression allows all numeric operators. If you create new
SQL functions that return a numeric type, you should invoke this macro that
type. Unfortunately, Rust disallows us from automatically implementing `Add`for types which implement`Expression`, under its orphan rules.
- [operator_](https://docs.rs/macro.operator_allowed.html)- allowed
- Implements the Rust operator for a given type. If you create a new SQL
function, which returns a type that you’d like to use an operator on, you
should invoke this macro. Unfortunately, Rust disallows us from
automatically implementing `Add`and other traits from`std::ops`, under its orphan rules.
- [postfix_](https://docs.rs/macro.postfix_operator.html)- operator
- Useful for libraries adding support for new SQL types. Apps should never need to call this.
- [prefix_](https://docs.rs/macro.prefix_operator.html)- operator
- Useful for libraries adding support for new SQL types. Apps should never need to call this.
- [table](https://docs.rs/macro.table.html)
- Specifies that a table exists, and what columns it has. This will create a
new public module, with the same name, as the name of the table. In this
module, you will find a unit struct named `table`, and a unit struct with the name of each column.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [copy_](https://docs.rs/fn.copy_from.html)- from - `postgres_backend`and- `postgres`
- Creates a `COPY FROM`statement
- [copy_to](https://docs.rs/fn.copy_to.html)- `postgres_backend`and- `postgres`
- Creates a `COPY TO`statement
- [debug_](https://docs.rs/fn.debug_query.html)- query
- Takes a query `QueryFragment`expression as an argument and returns a type that implements`fmt::Display`and`fmt::Debug`to show the query.
- [delete](https://docs.rs/fn.delete.html)
- Creates a `DELETE`statement.
- [insert_](https://docs.rs/fn.insert_into.html)- into
- Creates an `INSERT`statement for the target table.
- [insert_](https://docs.rs/fn.insert_or_ignore_into.html)- or_ - ignore_ - into
- Creates an `INSERT [OR] IGNORE`statement.
- [replace_](https://docs.rs/fn.replace_into.html)- into
- Creates a `REPLACE`statement.
- [select](https://docs.rs/fn.select.html)
- Creates a bare select statement, with no from clause. Primarily used for testing diesel itself, but likely useful for third party crates as well. The given expressions must be selectable from anywhere.
- [sql_](https://docs.rs/fn.sql_query.html)- query
- Construct a full SQL query using raw SQL.
- [update](https://docs.rs/fn.update.html)
- Creates an `UPDATE`statement.

## Derive Macros[§](https://docs.rs#derives)

- [Multi](https://docs.rs/derive.MultiConnection.html)- Connection
- This derives implements `diesel::Connection`and related traits for an enum of connections to different databases.

# migrations_macros - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/migrations_macros/~2.3.0/

This macro will read your migrations at compile time, and create a constant value containing
an embedded list of all your migrations as available at compile time.
This is useful if you would like to use Diesel’s migration infrastructure, but want to ship a single executable
file (such as for embedded applications). It can also be used to apply migrations to an in
memory database (Diesel does this for its own test suite).

---

# cfg_if - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cfg-if/^1.0.0/

## Expand description

A macro for defining `#[cfg]` if-else statements.

The macro provided by this crate, `cfg_if`, is similar to the `if/elif` C
preprocessor macro by allowing definition of a cascade of `#[cfg]` cases,
emitting the implementation which matches first.

This allows you to conveniently provide a long list `#[cfg]`’d blocks of code
without having to rewrite each clause multiple times.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
cfg_if::cfg_if! {
    if #[cfg(unix)] {
        fn foo() { /* unix specific functionality */ }
    } else if #[cfg(target_pointer_width = "32")] {
        fn foo() { /* non-unix, 32-bit functionality */ }
    } else {
        fn foo() { /* fallback implementation */ }
    }
}
```
## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [cfg_if](https://docs.rs/macro.cfg_if.html)
- The main macro provided by this crate. See crate documentation for more information.
